Import an existing data frame as a level

Source: R/levels.R
import_level.Rd

Brings a data frame into a fabricate call as a level of its own, so that real data can be crossed or linked with other real data. fabricate(data = ) starts from one frame and builds down from it; import_level makes each frame a named level, which is the thing cross_levels and link_levels work on.

Usage

import_level(data, ..., .id = NULL)

Arguments

data

A data frame. Its rows are the level's units.

...

Column expressions evaluated against the imported columns, as in any other level. N is the number of rows imported.

.id

Optional string naming the column of data that already identifies its rows. Left off, a column named after the level is used when the data has one, the way a join matches on a shared name, and otherwise fabricatr numbers the rows itself.

Value

A fabricatr_level object, meaningful only as a named argument to fabricate. It contributes the imported rows, an ID column named after the argument it is assigned to, and one column per expression in .... Like declare_level, it stands alone rather than nesting into the frame in hand, so it can be named in a later cross_levels or link_levels.

Which column is the ID

A level's ID column is named after the level, and import_level only decides what goes in it. Three cases, in order:

  • .id = "pid" uses that column of the imported data, renamed to the level's name. It has to exist, and its values have to be distinct and non-missing, because a level's rows are its units.

  • Left off, a column already named after the level is used as it stands: individuals = import_level(df) where df has an individuals column keeps that column rather than putting a second ID beside it.

  • Otherwise the rows are numbered, as add_level numbers them.

A column called N is refused. N is the number of rows the level is building in every expression it evaluates, so the two cannot both be in view; rename the column before importing it, or use fabricate(data = ), which evaluates nothing at a level and keeps it.

An imported ID keeps its own type and values, where a fabricated one is a zero-padded character string. That is the point of importing it: the column still matches the same key in the data it came from. It also means an integer key stays an integer, so a model formula reading it will treat it as a quantity unless you make it a factor.

Examples

individuals <- data.frame(individuals = c("ann", "bob", "cyd"),
                          ind_shock = c(-0.4, 0.1, 0.8))
periods <- data.frame(year = 2020:2022, period_shock = c(0.2, -0.1, 0.3))

# Each frame keeps its own key: `individuals` by name, `year` by `.id`
fabricate(
  individuals = import_level(individuals),
  period      = import_level(periods, .id = "year"),
  obs         = cross_levels(
    .by = c("individuals", "period"),
    Y = ind_shock + period_shock + rnorm(N)
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 6
#>   individuals ind_shock period period_shock obs         Y
#>   <chr>           <dbl>  <int>        <dbl> <chr>   <dbl>
#> 1 ann              -0.4   2020          0.2 1     -0.249 
#> 2 bob               0.1   2020          0.2 2     -0.926 
#> 3 cyd               0.8   2020          0.2 3      0.0342
#> 4 ann              -0.4   2021         -0.1 4     -0.829 
#> 5 bob               0.1   2021         -0.1 5      0.170 
#> 6 cyd               0.8   2021         -0.1 6      2.20  
#> 7 ann              -0.4   2022          0.3 7     -0.648 
#> 8 bob               0.1   2022          0.3 8     -0.582 
#> 9 cyd               0.8   2022          0.3 9      0.0863

# Imported units with fabricated units nested inside them
fabricate(
  villages = import_level(data.frame(villages = c("v1", "v2"),
                                     v_income = c(10, 12))),
  citizens = nest_level(N = 3, income = v_income + rnorm(N))
)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   villages v_income citizens income
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1 v1             10 1          9.53
#> 2 v1             10 2          9.09
#> 3 v1             10 3         10.4 
#> 4 v2             12 4         12.6 
#> 5 v2             12 5         11.4 
#> 6 v2             12 6         12.5
